## Before we get started

Today, we will cover how you can run a bioinformatics pipeline written in the
Nextflow language and developed as part of the nf-core initiative.
On this page, we'll introduce nf-core pipelines and do a test run,
and in [part II](w11b_nfcore2.qmd),
we'll run the pipeline on the @garrigós2025 RNA-seq data.

### Learning goals

Specifically, you will learn:

- Why you may want to use pipelines like those made by the nf-core initiative
- What the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline does, and when you would want to use it
- How to do a test run of a pipeline
- How to interpret the progress log and output files of a pipeline run,
  and the Nextflow final output dir vs. "work dir"
- How to restart a Nextflow pipeline run using the `-resume` option

### Getting ready

1. At <https://ondemand.osc.edu>,
   start a VS Code session in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`,
   with **4 cores** (you'll need these for the pipeline's test run)

2. In your VS Code terminal, create and enter a working dir for this week:

   ```bash
   mkdir week11
   cd week11
   ```

## nf-core pipelines and the _rnaseq_ pipeline

### Why run (nf-core) pipelines?

In [week 10](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#zooming-out-workflows),
we talked about managing complex bioinformatics workflows,
and the advantages that formal Workflow Management Systems like
[Nextflow](https://www.nextflow.io/) [@ditommaso2017]
have over DIY pipelines based on e.g. shell scripts.
While you can use Nextflow to build your own workflows from scratch,
we will here cover how to run an existing, community-developed Nextflow pipeline.

This is well worth covering for a few reasons:

- Available pipelines cover many types of omics data,
  so you may well be able to use one for your own research.
- Running such a pipeline is a bit different and more involved than running a
  typical piece of bioinformatics software.
  But when you know how to run one nf-core pipeline,
  it will be relatively straightforward to run others as well.

Recall from week 10 that the ["nf-core" initiative](https://nf-co.re/) [@ewels2020]
has many pipelines available for various omics data analysis types.
Here are their most popular pipelines --- we will run _rnaseq_ here:

![The 6 most popular nf-core pipelines as of October 2026](/img/nfcore-pipelines_2026-10-25.png){fig-align="center" width="95%" .lightbox}

### The nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline

The [nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq)
is meant for RNA-seq datasets like @garrigós2025's,
where reads are aligned to a reference genome to produce gene-level counts^[
As opposed to transcript-level counts,
which are harder to accurately obtain with short-read data.
Additionally, the pipeline only works when a reference genome is available,
as it cannot do _de novo_ transcriptome assembly.].

The inputs of this pipeline are FASTQ files with raw reads,
and reference genome files (assembly & annotation),
while the outputs include a gene count table that can be used for downstream
differential expression analysis, and many "QC outputs".
Let's take a closer look at the key steps in the pipeline ---
click on the image below to make it larger:

![](/img/nf-core-rnaseq_metro_map_animated.svg){fig-align="center" width="100%" .no-border .lightbox
  fig-alt="Metro map of the nf-core rnaseq pipeline, showing the steps in the pipeline and how they are connected."}

**Stage 1: Read QC and pre-processing**

- Read QC (FastQC)
- Adapter and quality trimming (TrimGalore or fastp)
- Optional removal of contaminants (BBSplit) and rRNA (SortMeRNA) ---
  off by default, but we will include the latter

**Stage 2: Alignment & quantification**

- Alignment to the reference genome/transcriptome (STAR)
- Gene expression quantification (Salmon)

**Stages 3 and 4: Post-processing, QC, and reporting**

- Post-processing alignments: sort, index, mark duplicates (samtools, Picard)
- Alignment/count QC (RSeQC, Qualimap, dupRadar, Preseq, DESeq2)
- Create a QC/metrics report (MultiQC)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Customizing what the pipeline does _(Click to expand)_

This pipeline is quite flexible and you can turn several steps off,
add optional steps, and change individual options for most tools that the pipeline runs.

- **Optional removal of contaminants** (BBSplit)\
  Map to 1 or more additional genomes whose sequences may be present as contamination,
  and remove reads that map better to contaminant genomes.
- **Alternative quantification routes**
  - Use RSEM instead of Salmon to quantify.
  - Skip STAR and perform direct pseudo-alignment & quantification with Salmon.
- **Transcript assembly and quantification (StringTie)**\
  While the pipeline is focused on gene-level quantification,
  it also assembles and quantifies transcripts with StringTie.
  This is run by default, but can be turned off.
:::

### Overview of running an nf-core pipeline

Here are some key aspects of running the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline
(and other nf-core pipelines) at OSC:

- We only need access to an **installation** of Nextflow.
  The pipeline runs all its constituent tools (FastQC, STAR, Salmon, etc.)
  via separate Apptainer containers that it will download for us.

- We can run the pipeline with a single command, `nextflow run [...]`.
  For our real run, the resulting main Nextflow process will
  **submit _many_ Slurm batch jobs for us**,
  and orchestrates these until the pipeline has finished or failed.
  Because the pipeline can run for many hours,
  we will **submit the main process as a batch job** too.

- Nextflow **distinguishes between a final output dir and a "work dir"** (by default, `work`).
  All jobs run and produce outputs in sub-dirs of the work dir,
  and only a selection of their output files are copied to the final output dir^[
  Typically, not all outputs are copied, especially for intermediate steps like
  read trimming --- and pipelines have settings to determine what is copied.].

- Nextflow pipelines can be **restarted** using the `-resume` option,
  which will make them rerun only what is needed.

### Test the Nextflow installation

We'll use Nextflow via an OSC module and not via a container.
That's because Nextflow itself needs to submit Slurm jobs and run Apptainer containers,
which is awkward from inside a container,
where the `sbatch` and `apptainer` commands aren't available.
(The alternative to to use a Conda environment for Nextflow,
but since a module is available at OSC, we will use that.)

We'll start by finding and loading the Nextflow module.
Then, we'll do a test run of the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline.

## Test-run the _rnaseq_ pipeline

### Introduction and setup

All nf-core pipelines can be test-run with a small test dataset that is included
with the pipeline.
Let's perform such a test run to become familiar with the command syntax and
the pipeline's progress log and outputs.

Unlike our real run later on, we will run this test **interactively**,
directly in our VS Code terminal,
and Nextflow will _not_ submit Slurm batch jobs.
Instead, it will run all steps "locally",
on the compute node that our VS Code session runs on ---
which is why we asked for 4 cores for this session.
This is a handy shortcut for a quick test run with a tiny dataset,
but not the way to run a pipeline on real data.

```bash
mkdir testrun
cd testrun
```

The pipeline runs each tool in an Apptainer container that it downloads for us.
To save time and storage space,
we'll use a shared dir with containers that I already downloaded ---
setting the `NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR` environment variable will tell Nextflow to
look there first for containers:

```bash
export NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR=/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/nxf-containers
```

### Starting the test run

Next, we'll run the test as follows:

- The `nextflow` command has several subcommands,
  and we use the `run` subcommand to run a pipeline.
- The pipeline to run is the argument to `nextflow run`, here:
  `nf-core/rnaseq`^[
  If we had wanted to run the _sarek_ pipeline, for example,
  we would use `nf-core/sarek` instead.].
- The `-r` option specifies the pipeline version to use
  (here, version `3.26.0`^[
  The most recent version, 3.27.0, requires a newer version of Nextflow
  than is available at OSC.]).
- The `-profile` option specifies which "profile(s)" to use:
  - `test` tells the pipeline to use its built-in test dataset
  - `apptainer` tells the pipeline to run software via Apptainer containers
- The `--outdir` option specifies the final output dir for the pipeline.
- The `--skip_qc` option skips all QC steps except MultiQC,
  which makes this test run a lot faster.

```bash
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq \
    -r 3.26.0 \
    -profile test,apptainer \
    --outdir results/nfc-rnaseq \
    --skip_qc
```
```bash-out
# [The output of this command is shown in the next section.]
```

::: callout-note
#### General Nextflow (`-`) vs. pipeline-specific (`--`) options

As you may have noticed, some options have a single dash and others a double dash.
This is because `nextflow run` commands distinguish between two kinds of options:

- **General Nextflow options** always have a single dash (`-`).
  They control how Nextflow runs the pipeline:
  e.g., which pipeline version and profile(s) to use,
  and whether to resume a previous run.
- **Pipeline-specific options** have a double dash (`--`) by convention.
  They set the pipeline's inputs and outputs,
  and customize which steps will be run and how
  (larger pipelines can have 100+ of these).
:::

After that, the output will provide information about the **processes** the
pipeline spawns, with one line for each "process" (i.e., step) in the pipeline:

- On the right (scroll right to see this), you can see each step's **progress**:
  - `1 of 1 ✔` and `5 of 5 ✔` mean that all of the step's jobs have finished.
    The check mark (`✔`) means that they did so successfully,
    while a cross (`✖`) would indicate that a job failed.
  - `2 of 5` means that 5 jobs have been submitted for the step,
    of which 2 have finished.
    The second number only counts jobs that have been submitted so far,
    so it can still go up as earlier steps finish for more samples.
  - `0 of 2` means that the step has started (2 jobs have been submitted),
    but none of its jobs have finished yet.
  - A dash (`-`) means that the step hasn't started yet.

- The **number of jobs** differs between steps:
  - Steps that process each sample separately, like trimming with TrimGalore,
    have one job per sample: `5 of 5` for the 5 samples in the test dataset.
  - Steps that only need to run once, like preparing the reference genome,
    have a single job: `1 of 1`.
    The same goes for steps that combine all samples, like MultiQC.

- The **hexadecimal string** at the start of each line (e.g., `[d2/97278b]`)
  identifies one of that step's jobs,
  and also the dir in which that job ran --- we'll get back to this below.

```bash-out-solo
executor >  local (29)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Additional info about the log output _(Click to expand)_
- The log only shows as many process lines as fit in your terminal.
  A line like `Plus 12 more processes waiting for tasks…` summarizes the remaining
  processes that haven't started yet.
  These will show up in the log once they do start
  (and making your terminal taller will show more of them).

- If the containers hadn't already been downloaded to the dir in `NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR`,
  you would also see lines about container downloads in the log.

- If a process line says e.g. `retries: 1`,
   a job failed but succeeded when Nextflow retried it.

- `executor > local` means that jobs are run on the same node as the main Nextflow process.
  (That's fine for this small test run,
  but for our real data, we will have Nextflow submit Slurm batch jobs instead.)

- Some steps only run for some samples.
  For example, `CAT_FASTQ` concatenates the FASTQ files of samples
  that have more than one set of FASTQ files (e.g., from multiple sequencing runs),
  which is the case for 2 of the samples in the test dataset: `2 of 2`.
:::

After some time, the pipeline should finish, hopefully successfully:


## The test run's output files

### Main output files

The final output files are in the dir we specified.
As you can see, there are several sub-dirs with outputs from various steps,
and these dirs are named after the tools that produced them:

```bash
ls results/nfc-rnaseq
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="ls-blue">bbsplit</span>  <span class="ls-blue">fastqc</span>  <span class="ls-blue">fq_lint</span>  <span class="ls-blue">multiqc</span>  <span class="ls-blue">pipeline_info</span>  <span class="ls-blue">salmon</span>  <span class="ls-blue">star_salmon</span>  <span class="ls-blue">trimgalore</span></code></pre>

The two most important outputs are:

- The **MultiQC report** ---
  this has lots of QC summaries of the data, both the raw data and the alignments,
  and even a gene expression PCA plot.
  Importantly, this file also lists the **versions** of each piece of software
  that was run by the pipeline.

  ```bash
  ls -lh results/nfc-rnaseq/multiqc/star_salmon/multiqc_report.html
  ```
  ```bash-out
  -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 2.9M Oct 25 14:17 results/nfc-rnaseq/multiqc/star_salmon/multiqc_report.html
  ```

- The **gene count table** ---
  this is used for downstream analysis such as differential expression analysis.

  ```bash
  ls -lh results/nfc-rnaseq/star_salmon/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv
  ```
  ```bash-out
  -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 9.7K Oct 25 14:16 results/nfc-rnaseq/star_salmon/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv
  ```

  In the table, genes are in rows and samples in columns, and the values are the gene counts:

  ```bash
  less -S results/nfc-rnaseq/star_salmon/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv
  ```

### The `work` dir

The `work` dir contains sub-dirs in which all jobs ran,
and where they produced their outputs before the pipeline copied a selection of
them to the final output dir.
It can contain many sub-dirs, and is often quite large:
only a selection of the outputs are copied to the final output dir.

For example, let's compare the sizes of the final output dir and the work dir
with the du command (these sizes can get *much* larger for real data runs):

```bash
du -sh results/nfc-rnaseq/ work
```
```bash-out
48M     results/nfc-rnaseq/
264M    work
```

::: callout-tip
#### `work` dir location
In this case, `work` is in its default location,
the dir from which you execute the `nextflow` command
(i.e., the current working directory).
For runs on real data, we will specify a different location for the `work` dir,
often on `/fs/scratch`, which is faster and has more space than `/fs/ess`.
:::

You won't need to explore these outputs most of the time,
but they can be useful for debugging or understanding the pipeline's behavior
and the exact commands that it ran.
Let's list its contents:

```bash
ls work
```

How do you find your way around that? 😳
As mentioned above, the hexadecimals between square brackets (e.g. `[fb/68d030]`)
that are printed before each job point to the subdir within this work dir that
it ran in (every individual job runs in its own dir).

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: Explore the `work` dir of the MultiQC process

In this exercise,
you'll take a look at the `work` subdir of the pipeline's final process: MultiQC.

1. Find the line for the MultiQC process in the pipeline's log,
   and note its hexadecimal code.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_</summary>

   The line should look like this,
   though your hexadecimal code will be different
   (so use the one from your own log in the next steps):

   ```bash-out-solo
   [fb/68d030] process > NFCORE_RNASEQ:RNASEQ:MULTIQC (1) [100%] 1 of 1 ✔
   ```

   </details>

2. List all files in this process's `work` subdir, including hidden files.
   Can you tell which are input files, which are output files,
   and what the hidden files might contain?
   _(Hint: the full name of the subdir is much longer than what's shown in the log,
   but you can use a `*` wildcard to match the rest.)_

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_</summary>

   Use the `-a` option to `ls` so hidden files are also listed:

   ```bash
   ls -a work/fb/68d030*
   ```
   <pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="ls-blue">.</span>    .command.err    .exitcode             versions.yml
   <span class="ls-blue">..</span>   .command.log    multiqc_config.yml
   1    .command.out    <span class="ls-blue">multiqc_report_data</span>
   10   .command.run    multiqc_report.html
   100  .command.sh     <span class="ls-blue">multiqc_report_plots</span>
   101  .command.begin  .command.trace  name_replacement.txt
   # [...Not all files shown...]</code></pre>

   The files in this `work` subdir include:

   - Input files (as links/shortcuts, so the files don't have to be copied in full)
   - Output files, such as `multiqc_report.html`
   - Several hidden files, including:
     - `.command.sh`: the exact command that was run by this process
     - `.command.log`: logging information from the process run

   </details>

3. Check exactly how MultiQC was run by the pipeline by looking at the `.command.sh` file.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_</summary>

   Show the contents of the `.command.sh` file:

   ```bash
   cat work/fb/68d030*/.command.sh
   ```
   ```bash-out
   #!/usr/bin/env bash -C -e -u -o pipefail
   multiqc \
      --force \
      \
      --config 1/multiqc_config.yml --config 2/multiqc_sample_merge.yml \
      --filename multiqc_report.html \
      \
      --replace-names name_replacement.txt \
      \
      .
   # [...output truncated...]
   ```

   It can be good to know how exactly a program was run,
   for example to reproduce the command outside of Nextflow,
   for your methods section, or for troubleshooting.

   </details>
:::

## Re-running a pipeline with `-resume`

When you rerun a pipeline with the `-resume` option,
Nextflow checks for each job whether it was already successfully run before.
It does so using a record of previous runs that it keeps in a hidden `.nextflow` dir.
A job is skipped, and its earlier outputs reused, if:

- Its inputs, command, and settings are the same as in the previous run, and
- Its outputs are still present in the `work` dir

All other jobs are rerun, along with any downstream jobs that depend on their outputs.
This saves a lot of time in situations like these:

- After a pipeline failed partway through,
  only the failed jobs and the jobs that depend on them are run.
- After you added samples or changed an input file,
  only the jobs for those samples or that file are run,
  plus jobs that combine all samples (like MultiQC).
- After you changed a setting that only affects the very last step,
  only that step is rerun.

Let's quickly explore how the `-resume` option works.
We'll first remove the final output dir,
and then re-run the same command as above, but now adding `-resume`:

```bash
rm -r results

nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq \
    -r 3.26.0 \
    -profile test,apptainer \
    --outdir results/nfc-rnaseq \
    --skip_qc \
    -resume
```

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>Before running this: how long do you expect this run to take, and why?</summary>

_The answer will be added after class._

<!--
It should finish very quickly:
all jobs had already finished successfully in the previous run,
and their outputs are still in the `work` dir, which we didn't remove.
So, Nextflow reruns few or no jobs,
and mostly just copies the final outputs from the `work` dir to the output dir again.
-->
</details>

The process logging should look like this,
where `cached: 1 ✔` (scroll to the right to see the full line)
indicates that the outputs were already present from before,
and the job wasn't actually rerun:

```bash-out-solo
[6b/1cecd9] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:GUNZIP_GTF (genes_with_empty_tid.gtf.gz)              [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
[6b/1cecd9] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:GUNZIP_GTF (genes_with_empty_tid.gtf.gz)              [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
[f7/9413a8] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:CUSTOM_GTFFILTER (genes_with_empty_tid.filtered)      [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
[f1/6ca0de] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:GUNZIP_ADDITIONAL_FASTA (gfp.fa.gz)                   [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
[38/a41513] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:CUSTOM_CATADDITIONALFASTA (genome_transcriptome)      [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
[4e/47e489] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:EAUTILS_GTF2BED (genome_gfp)                          [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
[63/c4489b] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:SAMTOOLS_FAIDX (genome_gfp.fasta)                     [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
[b4/886567] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:BBMAP_BBSPLIT (null)                                  [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
[da/47c581] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:STAR_GENOMEGENERATE (genome_gfp.fasta)                [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
[b3/c2208a] NFCORE_RNASEQ:PREPARE_GENOME:UNTAR_SALMON_INDEX (salmon.tar.gz)                    [100%] 1 of 1, cached: 1 ✔
# [...output truncated...]
-[nf-core/rnaseq] Pipeline completed successfully -
Completed at: 25-Oct-2026 14:17:07
Duration    : 2m 32s
CPU hours   : 0.6 (94.9% cached)
Succeeded   : 5
Cached      : 157
```

::: callout-note
#### It still takes a few minutes, and a few jobs _may_ be rerun

The `-resume` run is not instantaneous, though, because Nextflow still has to
check all jobs and copy the outputs to the final output dir.
But it is clearly much faster than the first run, which actually ran all jobs.
And for a real data run, the **time saved can be hours or days**.

You may also notice that not _all_ jobs were cached:
in the run above, 157 jobs were cached (`Cached: 157`),
but 5 were rerun (`Succeeded: 5`).
Such **"cache misses"** happen when Nextflow concludes that a job's inputs
may have changed, even though you didn't change anything ---
for example, because a step received files from many jobs in a different order,
or because an input file's last-modified time changed.
Downstream jobs that use the outputs of a rerun job are then rerun as well.
A few cache misses like this are normal and nothing to worry about.
:::

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>What if you had instead removed the `work` dir, and kept `results`, before rerunning with `-resume`?</summary>

_The answer will be added after class._

<!--
The entire pipeline would be rerun, taking as long as the first run:
Nextflow keeps track of finished jobs and their outputs in the `work` dir
(together with a hidden `.nextflow` dir in your working dir),
and doesn't look at the final output dir at all.
So, keep the `work` dir until you're done with a pipeline run.
Conversely, after a successful run, you can remove the `work` dir to save space,
as long as you won't need to resume.
-->
</details>
